question: How sure are the headline numbers: in which range does each stay when the test years and the basins are drawn again?
what: Bootstrap intervals for the headline numbers, from the stored forecasts (nothing trained). Test years, warnings at the high-flow level itself (names ending in _at_chosen_level, and at_level_chosen_on_validation_years in a verdict cell: at the warning level chosen on the validation years).
how_to_read: An interval is the range in which the number stays when the test years and the basins are drawn again: 4,000 times, 9 water years are drawn from the 9 test water years and 12 basins from the 12 basins, with replacement, and the interval runs from the 2.5th to the 97.5th percentile of the results (95 of 100 of them lie inside it). With only 12 basins and 9 year-blocks the intervals are wide; they show how much a number depends on which years and which basins it was measured on, and they are not a proof. They say nothing about rivers of another kind, about another region or about years unlike these 9, and they do not contain the difference between two trainings of the same network.

resampling.units: 9 test water years (2006-2014) and 12 basins, each drawn with replacement; a whole water year stays together
resampling.designs: years: only the years are resampled; basins: only the basins; both: both at once (the widest for 662 of the 666 statistics that have a range - use this one in the text)
resampling.designs_of_the_statistics_added_2026_10_: the widest for 1192 of the 1212 statistics added on 2026-10-08 that have a range (the sentence above is about the 666 of 4 October)
resampling.interval: 2.5th to 97.5th percentile of the resampled statistic (percentile bootstrap)
resampling.water_year: the 12 months from 1 October, named after the year in which they end; taken from the test period of flood.SPLIT (2005-10-01 to 2014-09-30)

monte_carlo_noise.what: How far an end of an interval (design both) moves with the random numbers, because 4,000 is a finite number of resamples: the spread of the same end over 16 equal parts of the resamples, divided by the square root of 16 (a standard error, itself rough). With another seed an end differs by about this much as a rule and seldom by more than 4 times this, so the last digit printed for an end is not firm. ends_near_zero: the statistics with an end closer to zero than 4 times its noise (an end at zero itself is not counted); whether such a range holds zero can change with the random numbers.

statistics_added_2026_10_08.what: the same figures for the statistics added on 2026-10-08 only (typical, largest, largest_for, n_ends_near_zero); the figures above are those of the statistics of 4 October, as then; ends_near_zero lists the statistics of both (those of 4 October first)

stat_names.<stat>.<set>.l<k>: set = a prediction set (see prediction_sets), or best_simple_w / best_simple_wq = the simple model chosen on the validation years for that lead (best_simple_model); k = days ahead. Each entry: value (the test years as they are) and, for the designs years / basins / both, lo, hi and share_above_zero (the share of the resamples above 0).
stat_names.nse_median: median over the basins of the NSE
stat_names.nse_diff_of_medians.<a>_minus_<b>: median NSE of a minus median NSE of b (the two medians can come from different basins)
stat_names.nse_median_of_diffs.<a>_minus_<b>: median over the basins of (NSE of a minus NSE of b in the same basin): the change in the typical basin
stat_names.skill_vs_persistence_median: median over the basins of 1 - squared error of the set / squared error of 'tomorrow = today'
stat_names.spread_ratio_median, correlation_median,: medians over the basins of the parts explained in spread_and_skill, for its sets: the same values as spread_and_skill.medians, here with intervals
stat_names.onsets_warned, onset_false_warnings, ons: an onset is a high-flow day whose forecast was issued while the river was still at or below the high-flow level (flood.flood_scores); share of the onsets that were warned, share of the warnings issued in that situation that were false, hits / (hits + misses + false warnings); the basins counted together
stat_names.all_warned, all_false_warnings, all_csi: the same three rates for all high-flow days
stat_names.<rate>_at_chosen_level: the same six rates at the warning level that 06_flood_analysis.py chose on the validation years (lstm_w, lstm_wq, lstm_wqf, lstm_wf, base_rf_wq, base_linreg_wq, base_rf_w, base_persistence; the levels are in verdict_stability)
stat_names.onsets_gain.<what>.<w or wq>: difference in the share of onsets warned, without (w) or with (wq) the river gauge: evening_rain_minus_base = with rain up to the evening of the issue day minus without; evening_rain_minus_control = minus the control (the same rain one day older); upper_bound_minus_base = perfect weather forecast minus without; lstm_minus_best_simple, lstm_minus_rf, lstm_minus_linreg = LSTM minus the best simple model, the random forest, the ridge regression
stat_names.onsets_gap_share_closed: evening_rain_minus_base / upper_bound_minus_base: the share of the gap to the perfect weather forecast (an upper bound that cannot be had in practice) that the rain up to the evening of the issue day closes
stat_names.onsets_diff.<pair>: added on 2026-10-08, for the pairs of PAIRS_NEW (see pairs): the share of onsets warned by a minus the share warned by b, the basins counted together (a fraction: 0.10 is 10 percentage points); the same two sets as in nse_diff_of_medians.<pair>
stat_names.onsets_gap_share_closed.<closure>: added on 2026-10-08, for the closures under closures: (share of onsets warned by the set - by the base) / (by the upper bound - by the base), the share of the gap in onsets warned that the set closes; the upper bound is a model that cannot be had in practice; <name>_beyond_control, where the closure has a control: (set - control) / (upper bound - base)

verdict_criteria.how_to_read: verdict = at the high-flow level itself, on the test years as they are; share_of_resamples_with_each_verdict = how often each verdict comes out when years and basins are drawn again (design both). at_level_chosen_on_validation_years repeats both at the warning level that 06_flood_analysis.py chose on the validation years (warning_level, a multiple of the high-flow level, kept fixed in every resample).

spread_and_skill.what: Per basin over the 3287 test days, then the median of the 12 basins; no resampling. Sets: lstm_wq = LSTM, past weather + river gauge; base_rf_wq = random forest, past weather + river gauge; base_linreg_wq = ridge regression, past weather + river gauge; base_persistence = 'tomorrow = today'; lstm_wqf = LSTM, past weather + river gauge + perfect weather forecast; lstm_w = LSTM, past weather.
spread_and_skill.how_to_read: spread_ratio = standard deviation of the forecasts / standard deviation of the observed flow (1 = as lively as the river; below 1 = the forecasts vary less than the river: peaks too low, low flows too high); correlation = between forecast and observed flow; total_ratio = mean forecast / mean observed flow (1 = the right amount of water); skill_vs_persistence = 1 - squared error of the set / squared error of 'tomorrow = today' (0 = no better than a copy of the last flow); kge = 1 - distance of (correlation, spread_ratio, total_ratio) from (1, 1, 1). medians['<part>_median.<set>.l<k>'] is the median of the basins; the medians of the parts need not come from the same basin. The same medians are in stats under the same names, with intervals (only the skill of 'tomorrow = today' against itself, which is 0, is not). spread_ratio_minus_correlation gives, over the basins, the smallest, the median and the largest difference of the two in the same basin.

notes: No model was trained here. Every number is recomputed from the forecasts stored in results/preds, on the test years. A warning is counted at the high-flow level itself; only the names ending in _at_chosen_level, and at_level_chosen_on_validation_years in a verdict cell, use the warning level chosen on the validation years. Before anything is resampled the script asserts that its sums per basin and year give the scores of flood.evaluate for all 45 prediction sets, that these are the numbers stored in lstm_all.json, rain_timing.json, flood_analysis.json, lstm_lobo.json, model_comparison.json, rain_to_midnight.json, aorc_rain_to_midnight.json, more_basins.json, forecast_input.json, and that the best simple model named there is the one with the highest median NSE in the validation years (58,767 numbers compared; 61,758 with the checks made after the resampling). All sets have a forecast for every basin, test day and lead, so every difference is taken on the same basin-days.

Resampling: the 9 test water years (2006 to 2014) and the 12 basins are each drawn again with replacement, 4,000 times, from one fixed seed. A whole water year stays together, so the days of one storm - and the same storm in several basins - stay together. Every statistic is recomputed exactly on each resample from the sums per basin and year; the first 2 resamples were also scored directly with flood.nse and flood.contingency and gave the same numbers. An interval is the 2.5th to 97.5th percentile of the 4,000 results: the range in which the number stays when the test years and the basins are drawn again. It is not a proof.

Three designs are stored for every number: only the years drawn again, only the basins, and both at once. Both at once is the one to quote. The other two show where the range comes from: for the median NSE of the LSTM with the river gauge 1 day ahead it is 0.560 to 0.627 when only the years are drawn again and 0.411 to 0.861 when only the basins are: which 12 basins are in the set matters more than which 9 years.

What an interval does not cover: how the 12 basins, the region and the test period were chosen (rivers of another kind, another region or years unlike these 9 can give numbers outside it), and the difference between two trainings of the same network (lstm_<set> is the average forecast of its seeds and is resampled as one forecast; the seed ranges are in results/lstm_all.json and results/rain_timing.json). With 12 basins that share storms and 9 year-blocks the intervals are wide, and an interval from so few units is itself rough. An end of an interval also moves a little with the random numbers, because 4,000 is a finite number of resamples: by about 0.002 for the typical statistic and by up to 0.007 for the headline statistics (a standard error, judged from 16 parts of the resamples; resampling.monte_carlo_noise), so the last digit printed for an end is not firm. For 13 of the 666 statistics an end lies closer to zero than 4 times its noise (resampling.monte_carlo_noise.ends_near_zero): whether such a range holds zero can change with the random numbers, so no sentence should rest on it.

LSTM against the best simple model with the river gauge (ridge regression 1 day ahead, random forest 2 and 3 days ahead; chosen on the validation years and kept in every resample): the LSTM's NSE minus that of the simple model, in the typical basin (median of the basin differences), is -0.008 (-0.024 to +0.040), -0.003 (-0.015 to +0.032), +0.006 (-0.011 to +0.045) at 1 / 2 / 3 days ahead. Every range holds zero and none reaches further than 0.05 NSE from it: with the river gauge the LSTM and the simple models show no clear difference, among the models tried. As a difference of the two medians: +0.033 (-0.043 to +0.083), -0.012 (-0.034 to +0.035), 0.000 (-0.029 to +0.053).

The same comparison in onsets warned 1 day ahead, LSTM with the river gauge minus simple model, in percentage points: random forest 0 (-3 to +4), ridge regression +8 (+2 to +14). The range against the random forest holds zero; the one against the ridge regression does not. (The best simple model, chosen by its NSE in the validation years, is the ridge regression 1 day ahead.)

LSTM against the best simple model with past weather only (random forest 1 day ahead, ridge regression 2 and 3 days ahead): +0.019 (-0.016 to +0.075), +0.032 (-0.008 to +0.115), +0.028 (-0.017 to +0.084) NSE in the typical basin at 1 / 2 / 3 days ahead; every range holds zero.

Onsets warned 1 day ahead, the 12 basins counted together (611 onsets in the test years): 17% (9% to 28%) with past weather, 19% (10% to 29%) with the river gauge added, 30% (20% to 42%) with rain up to the evening of the issue day added to that, 19% (10% to 30%) with its control (the same rain one day older), and 64% (55% to 72%) with the river gauge and the perfect weather forecast, an upper bound that cannot be had in practice. Of the simple models with the river gauge, the random forest warns of 18% (10% to 29%) and the ridge regression of 11% (4% to 21%).

Rain up to the evening of the issue day, with the river gauge, 1 day ahead: 11 percentage points more onsets warned than without it (5 to 18; above zero in 3,999 of the 4,000 resamples) and 11 points more than the control (5 to 18; above zero in 3,998 of the 4,000 resamples). That is 25% (11% to 44%) of the gap to the perfect weather forecast (an upper bound that cannot be had in practice), 24% (10% to 44%) beyond the control. 2 days ahead the gain is 4 points (0 to 8), a range with one end at about zero. 3 days ahead the gain is 2 points (0 to 5), a range that holds zero. In NSE the typical basin changes by -0.006 (-0.034 to +0.070), -0.005 (-0.045 to +0.029), -0.012 (-0.033 to +0.017) at 1 / 2 / 3 days ahead (against the control: 0.000 (-0.029 to +0.060), -0.009 (-0.043 to +0.021), -0.013 (-0.040 to +0.006)).

The perfect weather forecast, an upper bound that cannot be had in practice, with the river gauge: 46 (31 to 59), 59 (44 to 70), 62 (50 to 72) percentage points more onsets warned at 1 / 2 / 3 days ahead, and +0.246 (+0.021 to +0.385), +0.474 (+0.095 to +0.569), +0.499 (+0.223 to +0.575) NSE in the typical basin (+0.275 (+0.041 to +0.412), +0.501 (+0.137 to +0.604), +0.532 (+0.285 to +0.630) as a difference of the two medians). 1 day ahead the gain in NSE runs from -0.025 to +0.392 over the 12 basins and is below 0.100 in 5 of them: when many of those are drawn the median is small, and the range reaches down to +0.021. The size of what the weather of the coming days adds is therefore better read from the onsets and from the longer leads.

A river the model has never seen: the typical basin loses 0.126 (0.049 to 0.227), 0.086 (0.034 to 0.159), 0.064 (0.027 to 0.145) NSE at 1 / 2 / 3 days ahead (median of the basin differences, in training minus held out). The difference of the two medians 1 day ahead, 0.216 held out against 0.434 in training, is -0.218 (-0.316 to +0.064): the two medians come from different basins, and this range holds zero while the range of the paired loss does not, so the paired loss is the number to quote first.

Transformer minus its LSTM twin (same inputs and training budget, results/model_comparison.json): -0.001 (-0.027 to +0.030), +0.003 (-0.027 to +0.022), +0.006 (-0.025 to +0.013) NSE in the typical basin at 1 / 2 / 3 days ahead; as a difference of the two medians -0.018 (-0.055 to +0.062), +0.009 (-0.049 to +0.035), +0.010 (-0.029 to +0.024); every range holds zero: no clear difference in accuracy, among the models tried.

Verdicts when years and basins are drawn again (criteria of results/flood_analysis.json: GO when at least 70% are warned and at most 30% of the warnings are false; CAUTION when not GO and CSI is at least 0.40; otherwise NOT YET). For the LSTM with the river gauge the onset verdict is NOT YET in every one of the 4,000 resamples at each of 1 / 2 / 3 days ahead, at the high-flow level itself and at the warning level chosen on the validation years alike; with rain up to the evening of the issue day in every one of the 4,000 resamples at each of 1 / 2 / 3 days ahead. For all high-flow days 1 day ahead its verdict CAUTION holds in 83% of the resamples (GO in 7%, NOT YET in 10%); 'tomorrow = today' gets CAUTION there in 67%, and at its own chosen warning level (1.10 times the high-flow level) CAUTION in 70%.

Which warning level: verdict_stability counts a warning at the high-flow level itself. results/flood_analysis.json takes its verdicts at a warning level chosen on the validation years for each model and lead. For the 8 sets that have such a level here (lstm_w, lstm_wq, lstm_wqf, lstm_wf, base_rf_wq, base_linreg_wq, base_rf_w, base_persistence) the verdict and the shares at that level (kept fixed in every resample) are stored in the same cell under at_level_chosen_on_validation_years, and the six rates under the stat names ending in _at_chosen_level. For the 3 sets of its verdict table (lstm_wq, lstm_w, lstm_wqf) the two levels give the same verdict in 17 of the 18 cells (not for: LSTM, past weather + river gauge + perfect weather forecast, onsets, 2 days ahead: CAUTION at the high-flow level itself, GO at 0.95 times that level). With the perfect weather forecast (an upper bound that cannot be had in practice) the verdicts of that table hold, at 1 / 2 / 3 days ahead, in 99.6% / 89% / 56% (GO / GO / GO) of the resamples for all high-flow days and in 92% / 46% / 67% (CAUTION / GO / CAUTION) for onsets.

Why the peaks are too low (spread_and_skill; medians of the 12 basins at 1 / 2 / 3 days ahead): the forecasts of the LSTM with the river gauge have 0.821 / 0.620 / 0.536 of the spread of the observed flow, and their correlation with it is 0.772 / 0.576 / 0.511; the random forest 0.856 / 0.642 / 0.572 against 0.776 / 0.584 / 0.514, the ridge regression 0.790 / 0.579 / 0.532 against 0.754 / 0.575 / 0.520. A forecast that minimises the squared error has a spread of about its correlation times the observed spread: when it cannot know whether the rain will come, it hedges. In the medians of these three models the spread ratio is 0.004 to 0.080 above the correlation: about the spread that the correlation predicts, not exactly it. In a single basin the two differ by up to 0.215. Given the perfect weather forecast (an upper bound that cannot be had in practice) the LSTM's spread ratio is 0.974 / 0.967 / 0.962 and its correlation 0.931 / 0.911 / 0.886. The mean forecast of the LSTM with the river gauge is 1.013 / 1.050 / 1.069 times the mean observed flow. Basin by basin, the spread ratio of the LSTM with the river gauge minus its correlation lies between -0.095 and +0.137 1 day ahead (median +0.015). When years and basins are drawn again, its median spread ratio 1 day ahead stays in 0.617 to 0.944 and its median correlation in 0.635 to 0.934.

Skill against 'tomorrow = today' (1 - squared error of the model / squared error of 'tomorrow = today', median of the 12 basins, with the river gauge) at 1 / 2 / 3 days ahead: LSTM 0.210 (0.095 to 0.341), 0.338 (0.289 to 0.427), 0.357 (0.317 to 0.430), random forest 0.202 (0.101 to 0.314), 0.338 (0.275 to 0.404), 0.357 (0.295 to 0.416), ridge regression 0.216 (0.157 to 0.344), 0.333 (0.277 to 0.414), 0.369 (0.319 to 0.418); each value lies inside the ranges of the other two: no clear difference.

KGE (median of the 12 basins, 1 / 2 / 3 days ahead): LSTM with the river gauge 0.714 / 0.396 / 0.310, random forest 0.739 / 0.424 / 0.339, ridge regression 0.657 / 0.375 / 0.304, 'tomorrow = today' 0.717 / 0.504 / 0.435. At 2 and 3 days ahead 'tomorrow = today' has a higher KGE than each of the three fitted models: a copy of the river has the right spread and total by construction, so KGE is not read as forecast skill here.

'Tomorrow = today' can never warn of an onset at the high-flow level itself (the river was still low when the forecast was issued), so the share of false warnings among its onset warnings has no value: NaN, with null for the interval. In a few resamples another set gives no onset warning at all; those resamples are left out of the interval of its false-warning share (resampling.statistics_without_a_value_in_some_resamples counts them); in a verdict cell such a resample counts as NOT YET. The warnings of the drawn basins are counted together, so a basin without a high-flow day or without an onset in the drawn years adds nothing to either count; every resample has high-flow days and onsets.
runtime_s is the time of the whole script, including the checks.

Extension of 2026-10-08: 28 prediction sets and 60 differences were added to the 17 sets and 11 differences of 4 October, so that a range stands beside the headline numbers of the four experiments of 7-8 October. Nothing of 4 October changed: its 672 statistics, its verdict cells and its spread-and-skill tables come from the same code, the same forecasts and the same random numbers. Added, by script: 15 (the rain of the issue day up to local midnight, hourly ERA5) lstm_wqh, lstm_wqh_older, lstm_wqh_to09, lstm_wqh_utc, lstm_wqnh, lstm_wh, lstm_wh_older, base_linreg_wqh, base_rf_wqh; 16 (hourly AORC rain) lstm_wqa, lstm_wqa_to09, lstm_wqa_utc, lstm_wqa_rep, base_linreg_wqa, base_rf_wqa; 17 (63 training rivers, and 50 for rivers never seen; scored on the 12) lstm63_wq, lstm63_w, lstm63eq_wq, unseen50_w_static, unseen50_w_nostatic, together with lobo_w_nostatic and lobo_ref_w_nostatic of 05_lobo.py, the no-properties partners that its never-seen comparison needs and that this script did not hold; 18 (the GEFSv12 rain forecast, main split only) lstm_wqaF_sub, lstm_wqaF_clim, lstm_wqF_sub, lstm_wqaP, base_linreg_wqaF, base_rf_wqaF. For every added set: the median NSE per lead and the six warning rates per lead at the high-flow level itself, with a verdict cell (no warning level chosen on the validation years is computed for them: flood_analysis.json holds none). For the differences (stat_names.pairs): the NSE as the difference of the two medians and as the median of the basin differences, and onsets_diff in the share of onsets warned; for the closures (stat_names.closures) the share of the gap in onsets warned, to an upper bound that cannot be had in practice, that a set closes (a ratio, wide where the gap is small; a resample in which the gap is exactly 0 has no value and is left out of the interval, as for the false-warning shares: resampling.statistics_without_a_value_in_some_resamples). The NSE share of the gap is not resampled: its denominator can be near zero (lstm_wqaP minus lstm_wqa 1 day ahead: +0.029 (-0.094 to +0.264)). Every difference is taken on the same basin-days. Checks before the resampling: the yearly sums give the scores of flood.evaluate for the added sets, which are the numbers stored in rain_to_midnight.json, aorc_rain_to_midnight.json, more_basins.json, forecast_input.json (and lstm_lobo.json for the two lobo sets); the statistics of 61 differences and 19 closures on the test years as they are equal the comparison numbers those files store (gain_rule, closure, yardstick, unseen, gap_to_the_upper_bound); 174 verdict labels equal the ones stored; 22,124 numbers compared for the added sets and comparisons (8,292 for rain_to_midnight.json, 5,628 for aorc_rain_to_midnight.json, 984 for more_basins.json, 1,718 for lstm_lobo.json, 5,502 for forecast_input.json). Every one of the 60 differences has a stored counterpart to be compared with.

Left out: the sets of the retraining with the forecast (E2b; lstm_wqaF_s, lstm_wqa_s, lstm_wqaF_clim_s, lstm_wq_s, lstm_wqaP_s, whose names end in _s in results/forecast_input.json) lie on another split (test years 2010-10-01 to 2014-09-30: 4 water years, not the 9 drawn here), so they share no test days with the sets above and one set of resamples cannot draw them together. Their numbers are comparable only inside that split, and the intervals of results/forecast_input.json (uncertainty.block_bootstrap: blocks of consecutive test days drawn again) are the ones to quote for them.
